title: Sourdough Hamburger Buns
description: A naturally leavened hamburger bun with classic American burger-shop softness, sourdough flavor, and enough structure to hold juicy fillings without falling apart.
culturalNote: The hamburger bun is one of the defining breads of American cooking. Unlike crusty artisan loaves, a good burger bun is designed to be soft, compressible, and sturdy enough to hold juicy fillings. This naturally leavened version develops flavor through traditional sourdough fermentation while maintaining the tender crumb expected from a classic burger bun.
instructions: Combine the 100 g active sourdough starter, 220 g warm water, 1 large egg, 35 g olive oil, and 20 g honey in a large mixing bowl.
Add the 500 g bread flour and 10 g fine salt. Mix until no dry flour remains.
Cover the dough and rest for 20 minutes.
Knead the dough for 8 to 10 minutes by hand, or 5 to 6 minutes in a stand mixer, until smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky.
Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl and cover.
Ferment the dough until it has expanded by approximately 50 to 75 percent and feels noticeably lighter. At 75°F to 80°F this typically requires 3 to 5 hours.
After the first hour of fermentation, perform one stretch-and-fold by gently pulling each side of the dough over itself.
Divide the dough into 8 equal portions, approximately 115 g each.
Shape each portion into a tight ball.
Flatten each ball slightly into a bun approximately 3 1/2 to 4 inches in diameter.
Arrange the shaped buns on a parchment-lined baking sheet with space between each bun.
Cover and proof until puffy and slightly jiggly. Depending on temperature and starter activity, this generally requires 1 1/2 to 3 hours.
Preheat the oven to 375°F.
Beat the 1 large egg with 1 tablespoon water.
Brush the tops of the buns with the egg wash.
Sprinkle the buns with the 10 g sesame seeds.
Bake at 375°F for 18 to 22 minutes until deep golden brown and the internal temperature reaches 195°F to 200°F.
Transfer the buns to a cooling rack.
Loosely cover the buns with a clean kitchen towel while cooling for the softest crust.
Cool for at least 20 minutes before slicing.
notes: The dough should determine the schedule. Fermentation times vary based on starter strength and room temperature.
For the best burger texture, bake the buns the same day they will be served.
A starter that has recently come out of long-term refrigeration may require multiple feedings before reaching peak activity.
The finished buns freeze exceptionally well. Allow them to cool completely before freezing.
